utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody. Please be seated. Before we start, briefly for the record due to the change of the schedule of the bureau meeting, this case will be heard tomorrow not in the afternoon but in the morning, as usual from 9.00 to 1.45. Anything else for the moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wanted to inform the Court and parties that I have met and the Stakic team have met with those who are prosecuting the Plavsic and Krajisnik case. And after that, we have determined that if Mrs. Plavsic is a witness, as she is now scheduled to be, there is material that could be seen as falling under Rule 68 for Dr. Stakic and for that reason we have begun the process of making that available to the Defence. We will do that as quickly as possible. There are some logistical problems and I will also ask to confer with the Defence about some of the material to make sure they get what they need. But the process has begun and some of that material will begin shortly, and we will be working with the Defence to see if they can identify other documents that they believe will be helpful that are among the exhibits the Prosecution had listed for its case in the Plavsic and Krajisnik matter. There are literally thousands of documents - not pages, but documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. But before we continue. May I ask for the appearances. Sorry. I forgot it in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. This is case number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Nicholas Koumjian, Ann Sutherland, and Ruth Karper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Branko Lukic and John Ostojic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Any comments on that what has been said by Mr. Koumjian?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We don't have any comments, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I would just add this for the Court's information I do anticipate there may be a written response still forthcoming from the OTP once the full parameters of this search are completed. So we do anticipate still responding in writing to the motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And one final question of the basis of the Defence witness list updated as of 23 January. We find Witness number 38 -- I'm wrong in my recollection, but I believe this witness was withdrawn in the past. It would be your number 63. I want to avoid the name. I don't know whether ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, can we come back to this question after the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Of course. Of course. Only I wanted to mention this. From the same witness list, I take it that for the upcoming witness no protective measures are requested? Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No protective measures for this witness. You're right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May I then ask the usher to escort the witness into the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you then be so kind and give us your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. And as to the fact that you are called as a Defence witness, the floor is for the Defence. Mr. Lukic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Vila.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My name is Branko Lukic, and together with Mr. John Ostojic I represent Dr. Stakic before this Tribunal. For the transcript, would you please state your name.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: My name is Cedomir Vila, C-e-d-o-m-i-r, first name; V-i-l-a, last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When were you born, Mr. Vila?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: On the 10th of July, 1950.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Gornja Dragotina, Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where do you reside today?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I reside in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where did you reside in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Since 1975 to this very day, I have resided in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where do you work today?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I work in a shareholding company as a -- in Prijedor as a director of the company.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you please just restate the name of the company.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Shareholding company VelePromet based in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is your occupation, Mr. Vila?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I have a BA in economic agriculture.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where were you before the conflict broke out in 1992?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Since 1975 -- from 1975 to 1992, I worked for the municipal assembly in Prijedor as a qualified worker for planning and analysing. I took -- I took an exam to work in the municipal administration at that time. From 1982 to 1987, I worked as the institute for the economy and development established by Prijedor Municipality. I worked on economic analysis and economic projects. At the 1990 elections, I was appointed a deputy in the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor. At that time I worked as a director at the Sana Elegant company in Donja Ljubija, Prijedor municipality. From 1993 I worked in Impro, meat industry in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you for a period of time also work at the president of the executive board of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Yes, that was after the multi-party elections. Since 1997, in November I think, until the last elections when the switch was made to local government and self-government, I was the president of the executive board in the municipal assembly, Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In 1990, when you were appointed as deputy to the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor, which party did you represent in the municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I obtained my appointment from the SDP, Social Democratic Party, led by Nijaz Durakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is that a leftist party or a right-wing party?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: That's a leftist party. They're followers of the League of Communists at the republic level after the split of political parties within the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Usually when examining our witnesses, we begin with the year 1990 or 1991. I would like to ask you to tell us something about the result and insights that you had since 1987 when you worked in the institute for the economy and development.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: That was between 1982 and 1987.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Precisely. Will you please tell us about the economic situation in the country and in Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: At that time our state was the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia with all its republics and ethnic groups. The economic situation since 1970 -- between 1970 and 1985 has been improving on all levels. Prijedor municipality during this time had very important resources in mining, with the Ljubija iron ore mine as an important asset. There was the paper industry. There was construction. There was agriculture. There was forestry. So the Prijedor municipality was among those municipalities which had a medium level of development within Bosnia and Herzegovina. About 25.000 people were gainfully employed out of 115.000, which means that every fourth person in the municipality was gainfully employed. And the living standards at that time were quite satisfactory. In 1986 and 1987, a certain amount of economic recession could be observed. It was difficult to get new markets and employment steadily decreased. Unemployment was on the rise. However, citizens were still able to live off their work and retired people could still live off their pensions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Even as early as that period, were prices beginning to soar and was there inflation?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Yes, industrial production grew and production grew in general. So prices were beginning to go up, and the living standard began to fall. Nominally it was on the rise, but as you said, due to inflation trends the actual living standard of the population was sinking, and part of the population already had trouble finding jobs, finding work, finding markets to sell their goods and there was a disparity between the prices and -- between the prices and the market and the prices of the raw material, so the situation kept becoming more and more difficult every year.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At a later stage you were a director of a company in Donja Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Yes. It was the Sana Bosanski Novi branch in Donja Ljubija. They had between six and seven production lines. They were manufacturing clothes, mainly for foreign sales. Most of the persons employed there were women, and their ethnic background was decidedly mixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Until when did this company continue to operate, and what then happened?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: The company worked according to a plan and a programme and on the basis of agreed deals. The last jobs were finished on the 18th and 19th of May, 1992, and then on the 20th of May, 1992, vacations started, so the whole company took collective leave for all employees. Only the security remained in place after everyone else had left for their vacation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When did people come back from their vacation, and did they come back at all to work in the same company?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Unfortunately the company never continued to operate because, as you know, in our area a war broke out and foreign investors were no longer prepared to continue working together with us, and for that very reason the company ceased to operate. Immediately after the 20th of May - I think it was on the 22nd of May - there was a conflict in the Hambarine area which straddles the road -- the Ljubija-Prijedor road. This is 12 kilometres to the south of Prijedor. And for these reasons, the company ceased to operate. As the head of the company, I was trying to make sure that security and the janitors remained in place so that the production lines and the equipment there would be protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since the 20th of May in your company none of the workers were left aside from you as the director and the security. None of the workers came back, regardless of their ethnic backgrounds.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: There was our secretary who was a Croat lady, and she would occasionally come to do her job. And the security was in place too, and the janitors, I think, were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before April 1992, did you notice that people were leaving, that some new people were coming, refugees from Croatia, Slovenia? Can you please explain the changes in the structure of the population in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: One may say that throughout all that year, starting with the events in May, that is, from May 1991 to May 1992 there was an intensive departure of the population from Prijedor. Those who were leaving were mostly elderly men and women and also children. Since we all knew each other, we found it surprising that so many people were leaving, why so many people wanted to leave. And when we asked them why they were leaving, their answer was that they had relatives abroad and that that's why they're leaving, to go to them. And there -- when I said that we knew each other, we could identify them as being Muslims because we could recognise them by their clothes. Women wore typical skirts and scarves on their heads, and men wore blue so-called French hats with a pointed top. That's how we knew that they were predominantly Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did one of your acquaintances tell you when you asked them why he was sending his family from Prijedor and what was his ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: On one occasion I spoke to a Muslim friend, who told me that it would be good for my wife, who is a native of Serbia, and my son to leave the area. He told me that sometime at the beginning of April 1992, when my son was in the eighth grade of primary school, I told him I will wait until the end of the school year. Maybe then I will send him on holiday. And then he told me that he can finish school later on and that it was his strong suggestion in the best of his intentions for my family to leave, which was a sign for me that he may have had some direct or indirect information about the conflict that might occur in the area of Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: These buses, where did they go when they left Prijedor? What was the general direction where they went?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: They mostly were headed towards Croatia. I suppose that then they would go via Slovenia and on to the countries in Western Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before the conflicts broke out in Prijedor municipality, you were a deputy in the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor. Do you know what the role of the president of the municipal assembly is? What are his main tasks?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: His main tasks are regulated by the general authority and the statute of the municipality. According to this statute, the authority of the president of the municipal assembly - and I emphasise, the president of the municipal assembly - is to call the sessions of the assembly at the proposal of the executive board or the groups of deputies when this proposal is tabled by ten deputies. So in agreement with the aforementioned persons, the president of the municipal assembly establishes the date and time for the holding of the session of the assembly and he also establishes the agenda. At the very session itself, the president of the municipal assembly chairs the session, tables the proposal for the agenda after the debate on every particular item of the agenda. He then proposes the final agenda, the assembly in session, and the president chairs over that session. His other authorities outside the of sessions is to represent the assembly; however, he is not the superior or the boss to either the executive board or its president. He also does not have the authority over the secretary-general of the assembly nor its technical services. The secretary-general of the municipality is the person who has responsibility for the signing of everything that has to do with the technical services of the municipality, and he also proposes the allocated funds for the functioning of the technical services and the deputies of the municipal assembly. That is done once a year by the secretary-general of the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: A correction needs to be done in the transcript. I would like to ask you one question once again. Is it the president of the municipal assembly who proposes the agenda, or does he pass the agenda?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: There are different people who propose the agenda, and the president tables or conveys that agenda to the deputies. Then the deputies after a discussion and possible additions to the proposed agenda finally adopt that agenda at the beginning of every session of the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When people were leaving Prijedor in the way you have just described it, were some other people arriving in Prijedor from Croatia and other areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Due to the war operations in Croatia, a significant number of population from Croatia, mostly of Serbian ethnic background, arrived in Bosnia and Herzegovina to stay there or just use Bosnia and Herzegovina in transit towards other places, such as Serbia and Montenegro. According to the records kept by the administrative bodies, about 37.000 people arrived in Prijedor at the time. They were mostly Serbs who arrived from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know if refugees also went to other towns in Bosanska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Yes, refugees settled in all the places of Bosnia and Herzegovina and further on, in Bosanski Novi, Dubica, Gradiska, Banja Luka. There were refugees all over the place, and it is very difficult to propose a figure as to how many people actually went through Prijedor to go on to other places, but it would be my rough estimate that it was about 200.000 to 250.000 people altogether who at one point in time passed through Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You are now talking about the entire period starting in 1991 to 1996?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the 30th of April, 1992, there was a takeover in Prijedor. You were not a member of the SDS at the time?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: No, I was never an SDS member, nor at that time -- neither at that time nor at any other time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you continue being a deputy in the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I continued, together with a number of other deputies from the SDP party, that was my party, and also a number of deputies from the reformist party. We were all representatives of the left wing. I believe that there were 12 or 13 deputies belonging to the leftist parties who continued working in the local parliament of Prijedor after that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there a subsequent appointment of deputies to the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor and why did that happen?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Yes, it did happen. And that is due to the fact that the statute prescribes that the local parliament should have 90 deputies, and there was no way we could hold new elections and we had to have 90 deputies. That's why new deputies had to be appointed, and they were mostly appointed by the SDS, which is the Serbian democratic party. And I believe that people who were appointed were from the local boards of various villages, but there were also nine or ten other deputies who were appointed who were not members of the SDS. But I really don't know according to which criteria and based on which method were these people proposed and appointed to be new deputies in the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Your Honour, we didn't have time, because we were brought to this courtroom only a few moments before the trial started, so we have one list we received from the Prosecution and this list is the list about the events this witness is telling us right now, about the deputies who were from the SDS and from the other parties at that time and some were co-opted. So if the usher could help me and distribute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I can see no objections from the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, if I could look at the documents before, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please, first to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's not translated because we didn't receive the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I don't have any objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We will check. It's possible that a translation has been done in the meantime. We'll check the computer now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Maybe it's not necessary if we get some guidance on the headlines. The names need not be translated, because I believe we are able to read the Cyrillic names.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vila, since the Honourable Judges and other participants in this trial do not understand our language and cannot read the Cyrillic script, we will go through this document very quickly. Can you please read the title on the top of that page.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: That is a question to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: It says "Deputies of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor." And above that is either a "P" or an "R," and the number "0038366."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And underneath the title, how many names can you see?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: If I may take my glasses, please. Underneath the title, there are 28 names. Those are the deputies of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor whose mandate was verified in the elections, and then the next number 1 through number 41, those are the new names --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is the second title?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: The title is "Presidents of the local boards of the SDS." And their names are listed under numbers 1 to 41. On the following page are the deputies belonging to the DSS. There's two of them altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. I apologise. Just a moment, sir. DSS, do you know what the abbreviation stands for?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: The Democratic Socialist Alliance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is that a rightist, a leftist party?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: It is a leftist party.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The next title.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: The next title, "The deputies of the SRSJ." I believe that this is the alliance of reformist forces of Yugoslavia. There are six of them under that title.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was the head of that party before the war?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: In Prijedor or at the general level?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the general level.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: It was Ante Markovic. Then the deputies of my party, the SDP, the socialist democratic Party. There are five of them altogether, and under number "5" I can see my name. The next deputy is the deputy belonging to the alliance of socialist youth or the party of private initiative. There is just one deputy there, and then other deputies, ten of them altogether who belonged to other groups or parties. I don't know what criteria was applied when they were co-opted, but as I've already said, they did not belong to the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Under number "4," under "Others," what name can you read?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I can read the name of Mr. Radovan Krejic under number "4," in the group of other deputies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Your Honour, we would like to tender this document as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Maybe just before I have some -- I'll get some answers. May I ask you, Mr. Vila, have you ever seen this list, this list, a similar list? I didn't understand in the beginning. Was it provided by the witness or by the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: By the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: By the OTP. Okay. Have you ever seen such a list as you have it before you now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember ever having seen a list like that, but I remember the faces of the deputies as they were sitting in the sessions of the assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, could you tell us at which point in time this was issued or what's reflected here? Because on page 3, unfortunately the final line, it can't be read. It seems to be something like "93." Do you have any better copy? Maybe the question is in the direction of the OTP, providing this material.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From -- actually, it says "in total 93."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So you have maybe a better copy than -- page 3 at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll have that document and the translation brought down. Both -- there is a translation of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: At least by the break we'll have the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And just for another explanation, on number 1 you can read "Stakic Milomir, Omarska," and then followed by a column of figures. Do you know what these figures stand for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that a question for me, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The number in front of the name is the ordinal number. Deputy listed under number 1. So 1 through 28 are, I think, SDS deputies who had already been deputies prior to the drawing up of this list and they were appointed at the elections. The remaining part of the list, which says "Presidents of local boards," I think these members were co-opted from the SDS to become deputies, from number 1 to number 41 inclusive. And then the next page the deputies from the DSS, SRSJ, SDP, and SSO, DCSPI are also deputies who were elected at the regular elections, and then the part of the list which says the other deputies were also co-opted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. But -- and to have a neutral name on the first page, it reads, for example, under "27," deputy Kos," and then we continue and at the end of this line we see, as far as I can read, the figure 15295. Do you know what the meaning of this figure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume these are phone numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I don't have any further questions. Can we proceed as we did in the past. When we get the best possible -- the document, that we wait for the admission into evidence. Thank you. But not to be forgotten, provisional marked as D54B.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And would the usher be so kind and show the witness Exhibit number S191, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vila, this document has already been tendered by the Prosecution and given an exhibit number. This is about the verification commission verifying the mandates of certain deputies. So can you please turn to page 3. At the top of the page, number 2, it reads: "In the Prijedor II electoral district." Can you please read what it says under "B," the name of your party. And can you see your own name here?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Yes. It reads: "B, assemblymen of the League of Communists of BH/Socialist Democratic Party verified." And the fourth name listed is my own name, Cedomir Vila. My mandate is hereby verified.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will not be needing this document any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So we're talking about the period following the 30th of April. Immediately after the takeover, did a murder of a reserve police officer occur?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Yes. That was, I think, in the city district. At the entrance to the neighbourhood called Urije a murder occurred of a policeman whose name was Dzapa. I can't remember his first name. I think he was born in the village of Jelovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that between the takeover and after the attack on Hambarine a Muslim -- any Muslims were killed in the town of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I can't remember that event.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What I'm trying to say is have you heard of any murder of any Muslims or Croats in Prijedor during that period?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, I can't say that there were any such murders.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Apart from officials being removed following the takeover, could people continue to go to work regularly?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Yes. All employees who were not appointed to official positions at the elections could go to work regularly, and those who received appointments at the elections were free to go back to their former jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say your company continued to operate until the 20th of May, that is, the 18th of May when you finished your last work. Was anyone removed from their positions in the company between the takeover and the 18th of May?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: No, no one was dismissed, nor did I as the director of that company receive any documents that would indicate any such dismissals.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Even before the takeover, were certain blocks of housing facilities and buildings beginning to organise themselves, that's the tenants living in those blocks?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Yes. There were a feeling of insecurity in the town because part of the soldiers coming back from the front would carry weapons. Later on that was forbidden and they were no longer allowed to bring weapons home when on leave, but there were certain groups who were prone to looting and other such acts, so people were afraid that that would happen in their own buildings too. So in my own building, which has 16 floors and 24 flats, we organised ourselves according to certain schedules. We'd keep the front door locked in the evening and keep the front door locked until the next morning, and we had guards in our building. And if anyone forgot their own key to the front door of the building, we'd identify the person as being -- as living in the building, as residing in the building, owning a flat in the building, and then we'd let the person in.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you yourself take part in these guards?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Yes, I guarded my own building too, and all the people living in the building, whoever could took part in these guards. We usually did it in pairs, two by two, and no distinction was made along ethnic lines as to who would be included in this roster of people standing guard in the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did anyone force you to do this?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: No. That was our own initiative, the people who lived in the building. We had a council, a tenants' council in the building - I think that was the name - and we decided to have these guards of our own accord.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was this common practice in Prijedor during that period?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I think there were a number of buildings where similar measures were being taken. Some people locked their front doors and some people had night duties, but during night hours there was a lot of insecurity perceived and felt by everyone, and that was the reason why such measures were being taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you give us any names or ethnicity of people who took part together with you in guarding the building?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: On the ground floor of the building there is a room for general purposes, which is shared and used by all tenants. We would sit in that room, which contained over 100 chairs, and there was a chess board, so we played chess at night. I'd often share my shift with Mustafa Selman and a person who worked in urban planning as a project leader, Muranovic, I think that was his last name, Muranovic. I can't remember the first name. But that was the duty roster, and very often I would be together with these two persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time you and these other two persons you've mentioned, did you have a work assignment?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Yes. We all had a work assignment, and in our spare time or during the night we would guard the members of our own families and all the other people living in the building. So that was the whole -- the basic purpose of these night guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does the name Gojko Bojanic ring a bell? What do you associate with this name in the period immediately before or just after the takeover in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I think this happened before the takeover, in the first four months of 1992. I can't specify the month, I'm afraid. Mr. Gojko Bojanic and other two uniformed persons who were members of the army, they had been in Gradiska and came home, on home leave, and they were driving around in a personal passenger vehicle on their way back. As there was a shortage of fuel in that period, they took a shortcut down the Prijedor-Kozarac road and their intention was to go through Mrakovica and Gradac and reach Gradiska, that was supposed to be a shortcut because they were running out of fuel. In Kozarac, they were intercepted by a group of locals -- local Muslims who wore uniforms, and they were arrested and brought to the local commune building. Bojanic told me that some of those people yelled and shouted to have them liquidated, but a Muslim he used to know who did administer accountancy for him stood up against that proposal and he said, "These are just normal people, you know, common soldiers like everyone else." And then after an hour or two, they were released and free to go via Mrakovica and Podgrajci to Gradiska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before the conflict in Kozarac, did you travel to Banja Luka, and which route did you take?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: You can go from Prijedor to Banja Luka by train or by car, so the regular lines go by rail or by road. That was the most common way to go to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Between seven and ten days before the outbreak of the conflict in Kozarac, was it possible to travel down the main road from Prijedor to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: No, it wasn't possible for the simple reason that roadblocks had been set up along the road in and near Kozarac. They had checkpoints, and no one was allowed to pass through, no vehicles were allowed through these checkpoints. And those who did need to go from Prijedor to Banja Luka on business or because there was an urgent matter to be dealt with had to take a detour through Tomasica and then onto the surfaced road, has fault road in Omarska, and from there on continue to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it possible to move about freely throughout Prijedor municipality, or did one need to have -- obtain certain documents?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Throughout that period there was regular control, and if you walked about during the day you had to have some documents with you. So if you were a soldier, you had to have a certificate that you were on home leave from the army, justified leave. If you were just a common citizen, not mobilised as a member of the army at that moment, you had to have some sort of document showing that you had a work assignment. And it was common practice for people to be ID'd outside, about the town, or at the railway station, such places.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have a pass, and based on what?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Yes. The administrative body, that is, the CEO of any company, based on the number of people who were employed at the -- in the company or were at the work obligation would issue such a certificate containing the name of that person, the number of the -- that person's ID, and the job that that person performed. And anybody who had such a document would also need to carry an ID on their body all the time so that they could be identified based on these two documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When the curfew was introduced in Prijedor municipality, could you move about if you were in possession of such documents during the curfew?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: During the curfew, only soldiers wearing uniform and policemen on duty could move about. Citizens, despite having the document on work obligation, were not allowed and were not able to move about during the curfew.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That means you also couldn't move during the curfew.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: No. That would have been at my own risk. There was a lot of insecurity, and it was also forbidden, so no, I couldn't move.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you were to go outside Prijedor -- for example, if you had to go to Belgrade -- first let me ask you: Did you ever travel during the war operations to Belgrade or to Novi Sad?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Yes. After March 1993, I was the head of sales in the Impro meat industry of Prijedor. And because of the nature of my job, I did have to go from time to time to Novi Sad and to Belgrade. I had business to tend to there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What kind of documents did you have to obtain in order to travel to these two places?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Whenever I had to go to one of these two places, I would have to have a document from my company signed by the CEO of my company which allowed me to travel on behalf of the company. And if I was taking any means of public transportation, which was the most common case due to the fact that there was no -- there was a shortage of petrol. I also had to have my personal ID, and I had to have a certificate from the military authorities that I was allowed to travel. If I had not had such a certificate from the military authorities, there were a number of checkpoints before the border with Yugoslavia where people were stopped, and those who were not in the possession of such a document were handed over to the police. For that reason one had to have a permit from the military authorities to be able to leave the country. In that pass, there was an indication of time until which the pass was valid, which meant that it was indicated exactly when the person was leaving and when the person was supposed to come back to the place where he resides.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm -- if I'm waiting, that doesn't mean I'm not satisfied with your answer. I'm just waiting for the interpreter to finish interpreting your words, which takes a little bit longer. If you had to travel, where would you go to obtain such a permit from the military authorities?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: The procedure to obtain such a permit was as follows: One would have to go to the 1st Corps in Banja Luka -- actually, one would have to send an application together with all the accompanying documents. And once that was approved, one would receive such a permit with the signature of the authorised person on behalf of the 1st Corps in Banja Luka. Things changed a bit later on, and later on this document was received from Bijeljina and the paper contained the signature of General Mladic. But that was not his original signature but a facsimile that was stamped onto the document by the authorised official who was in charge of receiving applications and issuing permits based on the approved applications.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would this be an appropriate time, Your Honour, for a break, or do we have to go for an extra 15 minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I couldn't take it from -- let me just read. Yes. If it would be possible for you, then I would ask you to proceed as usual until quarter to 3.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To 4.00. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vila, can you please tell us, what was the time of the curfew? When was the curfew in place?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I don't know for sure whether it was from 2200 hours to 6.00 in the morning or between 2300 hours and 6.00, but one of the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I would ask that perhaps counsel could specify the time in the next question. I believe the last answer - not this one - dealt with 1993, and I'm not sure now when we're talking about the curfew if we're again talking about 1993 or 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The first line of question was on the procedure to obtain a permit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And I believe the witness had said that it was during 1993 that he travelled to Belgrade and Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yeah. But this should be, I think, clarified. It only reads that this was necessary but not in -- at what point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vila, the procedure that you have just described, to obtain the permit to travel, was it the same in 1992, after the takeover in Prijedor, or was one free to travel as they wished in 1992?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, as of May 1992 onwards, this procedure was in place for all those who had work obligation and who were obliged to travel.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One couldn't even travel to Yugoslavia for the first few months.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Yes. There was a lot of problems. The road was not passable for some time. There was no possibility to go there. Once the road was passable again, then one could start travelling there after the procedure that I have just described.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when the corridor was set up between the western part of Republika Srpska and Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, but I remember that it was a huge problem that Banja Luka was struck by disaster of the death of 12 babies in the incubator, who didn't have oxygen that could not have been transported from Serbia or in any way. It couldn't come by plane or through the Red Cross. But having said that, I really can't remember the time when the corridor was eventually set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You have explained what the curfew looked like every day, but can you set the time frame of how long the curfew was in place.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I believe that the curfew was in place during the functioning of the Crisis Staff, when the municipal assembly was re-established and started functioning again and when the situation was stabilised in Prijedor and around Prijedor, then the curfew was discontinued. But I can't give you the time frame of the curfew with any degree of reliability. I don't know when it was set up and when it was abolished, but I'm sure that you have the means to find that out from some official documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As far as the curfew is concerned, I need to ask you something else: Did it apply only to non-Serbs, or did it apply to all the citizens of Prijedor across the board?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: It was applied to everybody, and it was not possible to identify a passer-by who violated the curfew and such a person would be treated in the same way, regardless who that person was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear of the attack at the checkpoint in Hambarine? And if you did, what did you hear about that incident?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I've already told you that on the 20th of May, 1992 I went on holiday together with the other employees of my company and together with my wife and son I went to my native village, Gornja Dragotina, which is 12 kilometres away from Prijedor towards Bosanski Novi and Novi Grad. In that village I have my family house. I wanted to spend some time there to rest and to do some work in the field, which was my additional source of income. At that time the situation was very bad in town. There was a scarcity of food, and that's why I wanted to do some agricultural works in the field. While I was staying in the village, I heard on the local radio, which was Radio Prijedor that an incident had taken place in Hambarine. According to the report, an armed military structure killed one or more persons of Serbian ethnicity who were soldiers either coming back from the front line or leaving for the front line. This group of attackers was illegitimate group of attackers. I believe that one of those who were attacked managed to save himself. I'm not sure. Also on the local radio I heard a proclamation issued by the command of the army according to which a deadline was given to those who were involved in that incident should be handed over to the army or to the police. It was also said that if this was not honoured and if this was not done, there would be a military intervention. So this is what I heard on Radio Prijedor as something that was issued as the military command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... page 28, line 3 it reads "armed military structure." Wasn't it correct that the witness stated paramilitary structure?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He said "illegal."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Illegal, but not as it's reflected here, "armed military structure." Could we correct this in this way. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was paramilitary.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When citizens of Prijedor were leaving the territory of the municipality, did they have to settle their debt in respect of the utilities for the previous period of time?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Public companies such as the electrical -- the electricity distribution, postal services, water management did ask from the tenants to pay their dues. And those who intended to leave had to report to the Ministry of the Interior and had to report their intention to leave, and they also had to show the Ministry of the Interior the documents that they had paid all of their utilities for the previous period.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were all the citizens of Prijedor subject to this obligation?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Yes, all the citizens of Prijedor were subject to this obligation, but at that time the departure of the Serbian population from Prijedor was rather limited, that is, able-bodied men were not allowed to leave, those who were fit for military service. And there was also a period of time when their wives could also not leave because they were on work obligation. So the procedure was in place and it was identical for all the citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You worked in the Impro company, meat industry; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Yes. Since the 1st of March, 1993 I worked in the Impro meat industry company in Prijedor. We'd slaughter cattle and produce fresh meat and cured meat, and I was the director of sales in that company. So they required that I take up that job as my work assignment. Otherwise, they would have sent me to the regular army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: By looking at their documentation, at the documents of that company and talking to your workmates there, what did you learn as to how abandoned mobile property was treated? And I'm referring here to agricultural equipment, machines and cattle.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I talked to people from the commercial and technical section of the Impro company and to other colleagues who worked in the agricultural field in the municipality. I'm talking about the agriculture and vet station. I found out that during the combat operations in Prijedor and around Prijedor, a large number of cattle had been abandoned. There was stray cattle walking the meadows and all over the place. And the Prijedor Municipality ordered the above said institutions to start bringing in all this cattle, and the cattle that could still reproduce was then further distributed with certain obligations to agricultural workers. Equipment and abandoned machines were collected in a special depot where machines were then kept, machines and technical equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this would be a good time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stands adjourned until quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now continue, Mr. Vila?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that agricultural machinery was collected in a number of depots and that abandoned cattle was being brought in and collected too, rounded up and collected. Was anyone allowed to use these machines or the cattle? Can you please describe that.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Well, first of all, the Municipal Secretariat for the economy and social affairs was in charge and part of the responsibility of the secretariat was also the agricultural section. They rent out certain machines and a number of cattle to a number of agricultural workers. There would always be a certificate listing the goods provided and obliging the person who received this equipment or this cattle to take good care of it. And then as soon as the actual owners turned up, both the equipment and the cattle would be returned to their rightful owners.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the fundamental difference between something being lent out on the basis of a certificate and something being misaappropriated or stolen?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Well, the difference between these two is very significant. Whoever just took something or stole something, that would have gone unregistered. And it was very difficult to trace such goods and it was a big question if those goods would ever be returned. Whereas, with the issuance of certificates, it was all regulated, especially when talking about machines and mechanical equipment, when people returned to their place of residence, part of the machinery used for processing that had been lent out to the Autotransport Prijedor company, once the owner returned, the equipment was given back to the original owner. There were a number of other examples of this, but sometimes the period had been too long, so some of the equipment was no longer usable or functioning. Some of the equipment would be out of order or the cattle would have died, so it was pointless to give these goods or the equipment back to the owner. There were such cases too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I know you're not a lawyer, but do you know that on the basis of these certificates that were issued in such cases where the material goods could not be returned to the rightful owner, was there a basis to initiate proceedings before a court for indemnity, to claim indemnity?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I'm not a lawyer by profession, but it seems logical to me that if something was documented with a municipal administration organ, then the relevant body of administration would be under the obligation to pay the indemnities from their own resources. We did have such cases when I was president of the executive board later on, there were such cases of indemnity being paid out to people who had claimed money. Those were never particularly large sums of money, but still a certain number of cases were resolved in such a way that the money was paid out to the owners.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: A while ago you mentioned that you had had a work assignment. Can you please tell us, what is work assignment and what is war assignment or military assignment? What's the difference, and who is in charge of mobilising people?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: The Ministry for the Army or I think that's what the name was. The Prijedor unit, and then across the local units throughout the territory, they would receive from their own Ministry for the Army a certain document to commence mobilisation, and the grade, degree of mobilisation would also be announced whereby military-aged men within the age limits prescribed by the law would be issued call-ups, mobilisation call-ups. Their duty was to respond to the call-ups and report to their unit, the unit they belonged to and the unit would be specified in the mobilisation papers. This was specified in the call-up papers, the duty of a military-aged person to report to a certain unit at a certain time in a certain place. Everything else was done by the military command. That's in terms of disposition, strategy, and control and command of these units. Those military-aged men who had not been mobilised would be placed at the disposition of work collectives so that in accordance with the work schedule under the imminent threat of war or if there was a war, there would be a plan to which they would be assigned certain work tasks or assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you the following: Was it possible -- is it possible to simply refuse and say, "No, I refuse to be mobilised and no, I don't want any work assignments"?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: In practice it would have been possible, but this was also punishable and would have been punished, because according to the then-existing laws, a military-aged person had the duty to respond to the mobilisation call-up. And if this person failed to do so, the military police would be sent out to get him and bring him in. If this person fails to respond to the call-up or if the person flees from his place of assignment, this is considered as desertion and a punishment is envisaged by the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that you had been a deputy to the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor. What are your obligations, assignments, rights -- what were they as a deputy?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Within the framework of local self-government, we used the word "board member," and then "deputies" is for the republican assembly. But yes, I think we understand each other. After the elections and after the appointments were verified, the board member would become a full-fledged board member with rights and duties. The duties would be to participate in the work of the local parliament or in the work of the different commissions, boards, and bodies of the municipal assembly, and there was a symbolic fee, a symbolic salary for that type of work. As far as rights are concerned, the deputy would have -- would enjoy immunity while holding the position, immunity from persecution [as interpreted]. The deputy cannot be arrested while in office unless caught while committing a criminal act for which the envisaged punishment is above five years of prison. In such cases, the assembly could take away the immunity of the deputy. That's according to the statute and according to the local legislation that was in place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry once again that the transcript reflects that what you have said -- on page 34, line 7, it reads, "Immunity from persecution." I think you said, "Immunity from prosecution."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, interpreter's correction: Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As a board member in the municipal assembly, you're not an employee of the municipal assembly, are you?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Board members would usually be employed in a different place.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Yes. It would either be one of the companies or they'd be private entrepreneurs or they were just agricultural workers, which means that they would come from among the citizens, the population. But they would be given a legitimacy -- their appointment would be given legitimacy by the election lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As opposed to board members, the president of the municipal assembly and the vice-president of the municipal assembly are employees of the municipal assembly, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Yes. The president and the vice-president of the assembly are board members, and they have the same rights and duties as the remaining -- as the other board members, and their vote is worth the same. The practice in some municipalities was to have the president of the municipality as a gainfully, professionally employed person, and the vice-president would volunteer. But there were such cases that both the president and the vice-president would volunteer and they would go about their regular work in their respective companies but would be there for the assembly meetings and would preside over the assembly meetings and during the preparation of these assembly meetings. I can't specify now the towns and the places where this was the case, but had I known that this question would be put to me, I would have double-checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us assume because that was the case in Prijedor that the president of the municipal assembly was an employee of the municipal assembly. Besides receiving his salary as a professional and besides calling the sessions of the assembly and besides presiding over the sessions of the municipal assembly and besides proposing the agenda, does the president of the municipal assembly have any other right that doesn't belong to every other deputy in the municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: No, he doesn't have any special other rights, only when a delegation comes to visit the municipality, somebody from a higher authority. Then he has the role of a host together with the president of the executive board and others from the municipal administration who co-host such a delegation. So this is a representative duty. The president represents the municipality but not in terms of being able to sign contracts or engage in some financial obligations on behalf of the municipality and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So the role of the president, as far as I could follow you - and please correct me if I'm wrong - is mostly of the so-called representative nature?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You've also told us that you were the president of the executive board of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor. Can you please explain your role as the president of the executive board and your relationship towards the president of the municipal assembly, towards the municipal assembly, towards the head of the various services who were also members of the municipal board?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Yes. It is typical --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe this is -- the witness will be discussing a time period far after the indictment when there is no evidence that the same procedures would be in place during the time. I'm looking for the dates that he was the president of the executive board. I can't find them in my notes. I believe as Judge Argibay pointed out, it's 1997, which would be after the Dayton Agreement. And as counsel has continually pointed out, the statutes and the roles of various members of the municipality changed following that agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it can be clarified immediately, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will take into consideration the objection put forth by my learned friend. Since you were a deputy between the years 1990 and 1994 and in 1997 and 1998 you were the president of the executive board and there is -- that is a long time from the time period relevant to the indictment against Dr. Stakic, let me first ask you whether the legislation has changed and to what extent between the time when you were a deputy - and that was between the years 1990 and 1994 - and the years 1997 and 1998.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were the same laws in place? Was the same statute in place? Was maybe a new statute passed?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: There were no major changes in the legislation in terms of the organisation of the local administration. It was only after the elections which took place in the year 2000 that the law on local self-government and administration was passed and that law brought some changes to the role of the president of the executive board. So in the period between the 1990, 1994, 1997, up to 2000, there were no major changes in the legislation that would have a bearing on the local authorities, local administration, and municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In any case, even if there were changes, I believe that our learned friends from the Prosecution would point to those changes. But as we have you as a witness here, can you please explain in your -- during your mandate in 1997-1998 what were your duties, what was your relationship with the president of the municipal assembly, with the municipality, and with the heads of the various secretariats who were members of the executive board?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: When I was elected president of the executive board, the procedure was as follows: At an assembly session based on the interparty agreement on the distribution of functions and positions in the local parliament, there was a secret ballot for the members of the executive board, that is, of the president of the executive board, two vice-presidents - one of whom was a Serb and the other one a Muslim - and of the five secretaries -- various secretariats of the municipal administration. So one vice-president, two vice-presidents, and five secretaries of the secretariats make up the executive board as a collective body. The executive board in a regular procedure under -- which fall under the scope of local authority prepares certain proposals, decisions, resolutions, plans, and other enactments which are then given to the assembly for consideration. The officials of the municipal administration, that is, the secretaries of various secretariats, in keeping with the law, are in charge of the general administrative procedure and issue autonomous decisions. I can give you an example. For example, if somebody files a request to open a store or a shop, then the competent bodies of that secretariat will examine whether all the conditions for the engagement in such an activity have been complied with and if indeed all the conditions have been complied with, then the body will issue a licence for the performance of a certain economic activity; in the case, the activity of a store. So in their activities, they're independent when it comes to issuing certain decisions. The situation is the same in the construction where the secretary of the Secretariat for Urban Planning also takes into consideration various application, decides on the compliance with technical conditions, and signs licences and permits for the construction of various buildings and facilities. So the situation is the same in different secretariats, so the president of the executive board issues orders for the budget of the municipality, and it is only him and other authorised persons assigned and appointed by him who can subscribe to some financial obligations on behalf of the municipality, including loans. But when the budget is being considered and adopted, there are very precise criteria which have to be applied for various purposes. I don't know whether -- if I have to provide you with any more details on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you now tell us, please, who did you report to in your capacity as the president of the executive board of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I reported to the municipal assembly. The deputies then take the report into consideration and they either approve it or reject it or something else. The executive board, therefore, reports to the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever submit a report to the president of the municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: There's no need or prescribed obligation to report to the president of the municipal assembly. The cooperation between the Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 11298 to 11306. president of the municipal assembly and the executive board is cooperation in terms of preparing documents for the assembly. But this is not a binding obligation. If the two do not want to discuss this, there is no relationship of subordination, and the president of the executive board does not report to the president of the municipal assembly. Those two functions, those two positions are independent.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is the personal assistant of the president of the municipal assembly subordinated to the president of the municipal assembly or to somebody else?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I believe that I have already told you that the technical services of the municipal assembly are under the authority of the secretary-general. That means that all the employees, including typists, personal assistants, and all the other administrative staff which prepares the work of the assembly is under the authority of the secretary-general of the assembly, and the secretary-general reports on the work of the technical services of the municipal assembly, of all the personnel that is under him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You used a very unusual term in B/C/S. When you used the word that he accounts for and that he issues -- and he is in charge of the payment, what did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I meant that the payment of all the stationery, things that are used in the work, disciplinary procedure, employment, dismissal for those who violate discipline in work. So this is all under the authority of the secretary-general when it comes to the employees of the municipal assembly. That means that every payment that is made on -- in respect of the salaries, remunerations, or any material expenses -- whenever such a payment is made, it is done through the bank and such a payment order can be signed only by the secretary-general of the assembly and nobody else. That is what I meant when I said that he was the one signing the payment orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like to move you back from your position as the president of the executive board to the times when you were a deputy in the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor. You were a deputy as the time when Dr. Stakic resigned as the president of the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Objection. There's been no evidence that he resigned as president -- I'm sorry, I withdraw the objection. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was it that preceded that written resignation by Dr. Stakic? Do you know? While you were sitting in the assembly sessions, were you aware of any efforts to have him removed?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: At one of the sessions, there was a discussion of the resignation of Dr. Stakic as the president of the assembly and the election of a new person. Personally I believe that this was initiated by the party, by the Serbian Democratic Party, and that a number of influential people in that party asked for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would liking to go to the private session so the witness might mention some -- not the closed session. Private session would be enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I can see no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Although my last objection was an error, perhaps it would be clearer if we indicate that we're talking now about 1993, because there were two times that Dr. Stakic left office, and I presume that that's what's the question was directed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise to my colleague, and maybe he still thinks that he is in Brdjanin case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Should we redact the name from the transcript? To be serious, let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Confirmed. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will repeat my question. We're back in public session, so I'll repeat the question: During your time as a deputy in the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor, did you ever obtain information to the effect that the president of the municipal assembly had ever given any orders to anyone from the army?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: The army is a separate segment of the entire organisation, and I am not particularly well acquainted with how the army works exactly, but as far as I know the level of command and the level of organisation, the level of running the army, all of these things are done as the republic level, be it the Ministry of Defence or even superior military structures of command. So I don't know if there were any contacts or any requests, but even if there had been any contacts, they would not have been binding. And frankly, I don't believe the army would have listened to anyone in that position, because they are an independent autonomous structure and their superiors are at the ministry, and that's where their orders come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of the president of the municipal assembly ordering anything to anyone among the members of the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior is a civilian form of government, of authority. But then again, they're organised at the republic level. Chief of the Public Security Station in local community, at the local level, is proposed and nominated by the party, the party which has the right to appoint someone to that particular position. The Minister of the Interior appoints the chief of police at the local level directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does the minister merely appoint the chief or does the minister also decide who can or cannot become the chief? I will give you the example of Mr. Miskovic. So if you could please explain what happened.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Well, it was exactly the SDS that sent a nomination to the minister for the nomination, an appointment of the chief of police at the local level, and the person named was Simo Miskovic. However, the minister rejected this and then there had to be a new procedure and a new candidate was to be nominated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Therefore, the role of the minister is no mere formality. It's not a formal role. It's a role of actual power. He's the actual decision-maker. He decides who will be nominated and he appoints the candidate at the same time.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Apart from filing statistical reports to the municipal assembly, the Ministry of the Interior, did they have any other obligations to the municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior and the local police are in charge of keeping, maintaining law and order throughout the local community in their relationship to the civilian population and as regards traffic safety, as well as state safety. The public relations of the police and traffic safety are -- belong to a different section and state security is a different unit. So they brief the assembly. They send reports concerning the situation, the security situation at the local level. And you were right when you said that this is reflected in statistical data concerning events throughout a certain period of time. But aside from this, the chief of the local police could not have received any other orders or requests from the municipal assembly because the Minister of the Interior was his direct superior, or the Minister of the Interior's deputies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You as the president of the executive board, did you ever have the authority to order anything to the army?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: No, never. Except on the anniversary of a certain unit. Then I would go there to greet the unit. There'd be a cocktail party, a ceremony, that sort of thing, but nothing else aside from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You as the president of the executive board, did you ever give any orders to anyone from the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I did request some reports on the political and security situation and on the security of the citizens. I never requested anything else, any other reports, and there were no other contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This possibility of requesting a report from them, is that envisaged by legal enactments and under the law?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I am not a lawyer by profession, so I am not positive that this is regulated under the law. I think perhaps even not. I think this is more about the relationship between the local community and the republic organs covering the area, in charge of the area of police work, but I think that's the only thing that it can be.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the period between April and September 1992, did you ever hear of the existence of a body named Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Yes. During a session of the assembly - I think that was in late May, towards the end of May 1992 - during a session of the assembly, a so-called Crisis Staff was set up. The statute of the municipality contains an article governing the case of war or imminent danger of war, when the assembly isn't able to meet as usual and as necessary. The article says that the presidency of the assembly can be set up. I'm not sure why they changed the name from "presidency of the assembly" to "Crisis Staff." But according to its assembly mandate, according to the assembly rules what it's entitled to do is the same as prescribed in this particular article.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So the Crisis Staff took over the authority of the municipal assembly because the assembly was not able to meet. The assembly was a massive and inert body.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Yes. As we said, the assembly had 90 deputies, consisted of 90 deputies. Many of those deputies were away in their units due to -- on account of having been mobilised. So it would have been next to impossible to convene a meeting of the assembly. So there was this legal possibility to set up a body -- an assembly body envisaged in the statute which had the name Crisis Staff.
