So the Crisis Staff was in charge of the usual assembly work and had the same authority. Any authority that the municipal assembly had, the Crisis Staff had too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever attend any of the meetings of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: No, I didn't. There was an assembly decision specifying which fields of activity would be within the purview of the Crisis Staff and which people would represent certain fields of activity in the Crisis Staff. But aside from these people, no one else was allowed to participate in the work of the Crisis Staff. So I had no opportunity nor did I need to attend any of these meetings and take part in their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That is also the reason you don't know if there were any guests at any of these meetings, taking part in any of the meetings.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: No, I really can't talk about that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During that period, were Crisis Staffs organised also in companies or work organisations?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: In a certain number of companies and work organisations, Crisis Staffs were indeed organised. But those were arbitrary decisions by the directors of those companies. This was not something that was prescribed. You know, we had a war and people put on uniforms and they in a manner of speaking played out Crisis Staffs, even if we know that the company itself and the institution itself is in charge of these jobs and these affairs, both in wartime and in peacetime. So in certain periods, yes. But as far as I know, at some later stage this ceased to be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We discussed a subject that you found rather surprising. You didn't expect me to ask this. Why would someone want to say and what would someone mean by saying that Muslims were an artificial creation? Can you please tell us the history of how this ethnic group came about. That's as far as you know.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I'll try to keep it brief in view of the time and space at our disposal. I'll try to provide a brief explanation. In the Balkan peninsula, the influence of Turkey had lasted for over or about 500 years. Throughout that period, a number of Catholics or a number of Orthodox people converted to Islam in order to obtain certain privileges that were available upon conversion. In more recent times, since 1945, under the Communist system in the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, this question was not brought up very often, and according to certain systems of distribution of power and positions, according to the so-called national key, these issues were kept at bay. However, the status of Muslims over the last 40 years was different. And I will try to show this by quoting the fact that they -- by the way they declared themselves at regular censuses every ten years. In 1961, in the 1961 census, Muslims could either declare themselves as Serbs or as Croats. There was no third option available to them. In the 1971 census, a term "non-applicable" was invented, but it was still open to Muslims to declare themselves as Serbs or as Croats. In 1971 and 1991, they declared themselves as Muslims -- in 1981 and 1991. Most recently, we've seen the term "Bosniak" used, widely used. So all of this was imposed in order to establish certain distinctions among people, although there were no actual distinctions on the ground because Serbs, Croats, and Muslims speak the same language. So this issue was more imposed from outside. It was not an actual problem on the ground. This statement about the artificial creation of Muslims as a nation I think might be based on some of these elements that I've just referred to or perhaps on some others.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're not getting the interpretation. There's a technical problem. I see the interpreter speaking, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you please try again.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. We can proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This didn't go down on the transcript, so I'll repeat my question. Did you know the late Mr. Simo Drljaca? How well did you know him and for how long? What can you tell us about him?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I had known Mr. Simo Drljaca since 1980, when he worked as a lawyer in the centre for elementary education. I knew him later too. He was a rather brusque abrupt man. His nature was abrupt. He wanted to always be in the foreground of things, and he wanted to always be the first, to gain as much prominence as possible. I shouldn't speak ill of a dead person, but I think it must be said that he was an abrupt, brusque, even arrogant person and that he was a domineering person too, with a tendency to dominate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, what is the meaning and how we in Bosnia interpret it and how was it prescribed by the constitution -- what is the meaning of the term "constitutionality of the people"?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: This is -- this belongs to the area of constitutional law. But for people to be a constitutive people, that people has to be -- when changes in the constitution are made, there should be a majority of the positively expressed opinion of that people and other peoples as well. In the concrete situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, this principle was not honoured.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, for this. We had to contact our investigators during the break, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you aware of the fact that in order to change the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina a majority had to be in favour of each of the peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina that are known and that exist as constitutive people of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, first the form of the question makes it sound like Mr. Lukic is testifying. I'm sure he doesn't want to. And this witness is not a constitutional law expert nor is that issue relevant to this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Following deliberations, sustained for the same reasons given when witnesses were asked similar questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A very specific question: Do you know how many representatives of the Serbian people remained as deputies in the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina after the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina was abandoned by the representatives of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Except for the information that I obtained from the media, I don't have any other information. I believe that very few Serbian representatives remained in the BH parliament after that. I can't tell you with any degree of reliability whether the number was three or four representatives altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know that Dr. Stakic was not a member of the SDS but of another party? And if you did, did you also know what party that was? I'm talking about the time before the elections which took place in 1990.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I met Dr. Stakic as a fellow deputy. And when candidates were proposed, I know that he was proposed on behalf of the SDS. I learnt later on from others that he was a representative of the Radical Party but not of the Serbian Radical Party but of the party headed by lawyer Guberina, who was on the list of candidates for the constituency of Omarska, and Omarska gave the majority of its votes to that party and to that particular candidate of theirs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Although you were not an SDS member, did you know at the time of the conflict between Simo Miskovic and Milomir Stakic and of the conflict between Srdjo Srdic and Milomir Stakic?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I never attended any official SDS meetings, so I don't know the origins of certain conflicts. But I know that during assembly sessions when certain issues were discussed, that the most criticisms and most attacks on Dr. Stakic came from these two people that you have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You didn't know Dr. Stakic before 1990; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: That is correct. I met him at the first assembly session, and later on I saw him at the subsequent assembly sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you first met Dr. Stakic, did you have an opinion -- did you make an opinion of him?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Yes. When he was presiding over the parliament and when he was deciding the positions of the municipal assembly, he took into account all the individual opinions. The impression I had of him was of a peaceful person and a correct person. I don't know him privately as a family man, but I believe that his life is focussed on two things: One is his life of his profession, that is, his medical profession; and the other is his love of his family. You couldn't notice any kinds of extreme behaviour or arrogance in any field of his work or anything that he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear Dr. Stakic speaking on TV or on radio?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: At that time there was no local television in Prijedor, so such an appearance would have been impossible. We have a local radio and a local paper, Kozarski Vjesnik. As far as I followed these two media, I didn't notice Dr. Stakic appearing in the media that would result in bad relationships or that would discriminate against any particular people or ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vila. This is the end of my examination-in-chief. And now my learned friends from the Prosecution will have questions to ask you, and after them the Honourable Judges. Thank you once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stands adjourned until quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Before we start cross-examination, the Judge parties and the Judges were provided with D54. Any objections as regards the admission into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. That's the one -- no, Your Honour. That was the 65 ter number 454, yes? That was the Defence exhibit today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. So 65 ter number 454, which is now D54 A and B respectively, admitted into evidence. Mr. Koumjian, you may start.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, are you offended yourself by the remark of referring to Muslims as an artificial nation or artificially created?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I think that if one says that Muslims are an artificial creation, that this was not meant to offend an ethnic group as a whole. It was just to put them in perspective as regards other people, their origins, as the people were not similar, as people who have a religion, that is, Muslim religion. They have the chronology of their origin. But in terms of their ethnicity, they don't have a long tradition or deep roots. Personally, I would never offend any member of any ethnic group, and my attempt to provide you with a brief origin of that ethnic group was just my attempt to give you the history within a time perspective of the origins of the people who share the same language and share the same territory where they live, without having a long history or deep roots of their origin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So would you use the same expression in speaking publicly? Would you refer to Muslims as being artificially created?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: In the philosophical or theoretical circles, this would call for a long discussion. But in more specific terms, my attempt to elaborate this thing is my attempt to explain what Dr. Stakic meant when he said that on one occasion. I believe that it wasn't my -- his intention or my elaboration to offend anybody but just to put things in the time perspective. How could one call these people? Are they the people who do not declare themselves as any ethnic group? Are they Muslims? Are they Bosniaks? I believe it is for somebody else to decide that. But I as a person have nothing against this ethnic group, against their customs, their religion, their right to organise themselves, and I am trying to just explain things and I would kindly ask you to understand that in the way I have meant it and I have said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, and I'd kindly ask you to try to limit your answers to the exact question that I -- that you answer the question that I ask. Sir, you indicated in the answer that you did give that Dr. Stakic said this on one occasion. Did you hear him say this?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I believe that it appeared in an article, in a newspaper, in the local newspaper, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you recall reading that?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: This does ring a bell. I don't know whether I have personally read it or somebody who has read it told me about it. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, and would I be correct in assuming that you are not a Bosniak, you are not a Muslim yourself?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: No, I am not. But this is not something that is predetermined for anybody in advance. This is what you are given at birth. And a person, an individual, is not either guilty or doesn't take any credits for being a member of a certain ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, what is your ethnicity? How do you identify yourself?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I am a Serb, and that's how I identify myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, having lived in Bosnia for your entire life and for most of it in Prijedor, have you ever met a Muslim who would describe Muslims as being -- or Bosniaks as being artificially created?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I have known a number of Muslims. I met them in primary school, in secondary school, at the university. A lot of them have been my colleagues in the workplace. And let me tell you, I've never discussed that with any of them, nor did we ever think that that might become a problem. However, the frequent changes that they have been given to them by way of the way they declare themselves obviously reflect those dilemmas. I have already told you what possibilities they have been given in various censuses, and they have not been given a continuity when declaring themselves as members of a certain ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So your answer to my question, which was: Have you ever heard a Muslim describe or a Bosniak describe their race as being artificially created, the answer, the truth is, you've never heard them describe themselves in that way. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Sir, on the 30th -- excuse me. In the 1990 elections, you were elected to the Prijedor Municipal Assembly. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And you told us that was from the -- I believe it's the social democratic Party - correct me if I'm giving the name of the party wrong, but the former -- the successor more or less to the Communist party in the former Yugoslavia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And this was a multi-ethnic party. You had individuals from different ethnicities within a multi-ethnic assembly. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In those elections in 1990, who was allowed to vote? Was a particular group vote allowed to vote or were all ethnicities allowed to vote if they met the age qualifications?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: All those who had the right to vote.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In those elections, 90 members of the assembly were elected, of which 28 belonged to the SDS party. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And there was 30 deputies for the SDA and, I believe, 2 deputies for the HDZ. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Two -- two from the HDZ, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you told us that after the 30th of April, 1992, you continued - and I could find the exact page of the transcript - you were asked by Mr. Lukic at 14.42.06. It's page 4 of -- well, I don't have the correct pagination because I have it from an e-mail. You were asked: "Did you continue --" this is after the 30th of April. "Did you continue being a deputy in the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor?" And you answered, "I continued together with a number of other deputies from the SDP party, that was my party, and also a number of deputies from the reformist party." Sir, the municipal that was elected never met again after the takeover. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I don't think I understood your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. I'll try to make it more clear. The body that you were elected to was a multi-ethnic assembly representing all the voters in Prijedor. The assembly that you continued in after the 30th of April was only an assembly put together by the SDS party and excluding the representatives of the Muslim and Croat communities. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I am not sure whether the possibility was given to the elected deputies of the SDA and the HDZ to continue as deputies. I think the reason is that their choice was to no longer participate in the work of the assembly. However, according to the election rules and the duties of the deputies, it says that a deputy is supposed to respect the rights of people who gave him votes, and I followed this instruction. I was appointed for a term of four years, and I stayed in the assembly for a full four years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, that takeover that we've talked about, that was a coup by force against the elected government. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I don't think I could respond precisely to your chronology [as interpreted], the chronology [as interpreted] as offered by you. It's obvious that there was a takeover. But when the assembly was supposed to continue its work, there was a session and all of the deputies who chose to remain and to continue to work for the local parliament, we were told that the dispatch from the Minister of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- I'm not sure, but I think his name was Delimustafic -- suggested that roadblocks be set up and that an evacuation be started of the former JNA from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina in order, so it said, to avoid war. This attempt to engage me and other deputies in the assembly was aimed exactly at this, to ensure -- to secure continuity of work for the assembly without jeopardising anyone's rights and in keeping with the rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. On page 58, line 12 and 13, it reads "chronology." But I think the witness said "terminology." Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you for the correction. The witness said "terminology."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, sir, what was it in my terminology that you disagreed with? I used the word "coup." Did you explain to us why you don't agree with that term.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I spoke about my own participation and about the participation of others in the parliament. Personally, myself as well as a number of other deputies had nothing to do with this action or this activity. Our work was only about participating in the work of the parliament, the local assembly of Prijedor. The circumstances that arose, there was no way for us to influence them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I'll come to your role in just a moment. But now I'm talk about the takeover. That was -- do you have any problem with the terminology coup? Do you disagree with that in any way?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Well, as far as I'm familiar with the term "coup," the term would imply a violent takeover. And when I say "violent takeover," that means victims, casualties, damage, destruction, which was not the case in Prijedor. Yes, there was a takeover, but there was not a single victim or casualty. So I think "coup" is too extreme a term for what happened in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, in that takeover, was it accomplished by the use of arms and by the use of overwhelming force? I'm not asking if anyone was shot, but was it accomplished by the deployment of armed men at all the strategic points in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: As far as I know, the municipal assembly building was taken. And aside from the appointed officials, all of the others who worked in the other services and units in the assembly could continue their work. The only exception to this were Muslim appointed officials. But the explanation provided was that this had been done in order to avoid conflict related to the document that I have referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, the armed takeover, if I may use that terminology, installed a new government and new assembly and replaced, evicted, the elected assembly of Prijedor. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I'm not sure if you could say "evicted." I'd say, rather, that part of the elected assembly and deputies refused to work on, under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, let's take, for example, Professor Cehajic. You know that by the time you were working in the assembly, he was in the Omarska -- he was either in the Omarska camp or had disappeared from the camp, correct, by the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: As far as I know, Mr. Cehajic was a teacher of Serbo-Croatian at a local secondary school, and then he was appointed as the president of the municipal assembly on behalf of the SDA. Once he was no longer to perform his position as the president, as far as I know he was free to return to the secondary school as a teacher. Now, as to whether, where, and how he went missing, or if anything bad happened to him, I really don't have any information on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, how many members of the left bloc cooperated with the SDS in the government that took over Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I wouldn't call it cooperation with the SDS. I think that was just the continuation of the work of a certain number of deputies in a changed make-up of the assembly. The document that one received at the first session of the assembly, of the new assembly with the new make-up, the first session, as far as I can remember, was attended by 13 deputies from all those parties which were not national parties or did not identify themselves as national parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So that would be 13 out of 30 deputies attended. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And how many of those were not of Serbian ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: The document provides an accurate list with first and last names. You can use this to identify the ethnic background of each of the deputies attending. I can't be sure now when I speak about it whether among the remaining parties from the left bloc there were any non-Serb deputies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So you cannot recall now the name of any non-Serb who participated in the post-takeover government.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What was the position of Risto Banovic in your party?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Risto Banovic was a member of the party. He was an elected deputy. He had the status of a deputy. He didn't have any other special status.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Dr. Banovic did not participate in the assembly after the takeover. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Banovic is a psychologist by profession, and I cannot claim with any certainty whether he continued to work after the takeover or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, and if I could just ask you not to add information that's not relevant to the question, just in the interests of time. Among the people that were not members of the nationalist parties was Mr. Murselovic of the Party of Private Initiative. Was he invited to attend the meetings of your post-takeover assembly?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: My status was as a deputy at the assembly, and after I received my invitation, I responded to it. Now, whether the organisers of the assembly session sent out an invitation to the people you refer to, I really can't say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And I understand from your testimony on direct examination that the responsibility for convening these meetings was the responsibility of the president of the assembly. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: The president of the assembly, upon the proposal of the proposer, sets a date for the meeting and prepares the meeting. But then the technical part of the preparation is carried out by the secretary-general of the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you understand it as part of the responsibilities of the president to make sure that the members are invited to a meeting that he convenes?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: At a session of the assembly, the secretary of the assembly would inform the deputies -- the board members, correction, whether all the documents related to the assembly meeting have been sent out to all the participants, to all the deputies, and he informs also the president and all the participants about the attendance at the session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know if Dr. Stakic or any member of the technical service made any attempt to invite the deputies who were being held in the Omarska camp to come to the assembly meetings?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I don't know whether the deputies were in any of the camps or collection centres, depending on how you use the terminology. But it is quite obvious that the deputies had their own private addresses, places of residence, and I do assume that invitations were sent out to them. However, I am a deputy but I'm not professionally involved with this particular service. I just don't have the information you're asking me about, whether this was done or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. As a deputy of the assembly, did you view it as part of your duties to be informed about the most important events happening to the people of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: During the work of the assembly, during the sessions, I was a deputy belonging to one of the opposition parties and I did raise issues quite often and I demanded answers. Very often I found myself in disagreement with the general tone of the discussion or the matters brought up. But specifically when the assembly resumed work, it was said and the reasons were given that I have already described, that in order to secure the continuation of the assembly's work, that's what was done, and what they told us is that a certain dispatch from the minister indicated the possibility of roadblocks being set up or a forced evacuation of the JNA, perhaps even laying siege to the JNA barracks. It was for these reasons, to prevent war from breaking out. Myself and part of other deputies from the left bloc agreed to continue working in the municipal assembly, firstly; and secondly, as I've already stated, out of regard and respect for the voters who voted us in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. I was going to come to that later, but let me talk about the -- let me talk about some other matters right now. Sorry. Sir, at that time, the 30th of April, 1992, was the JNA viewed by the Serbian residents of Prijedor as being sympathetic to their cause?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Well, in my opinion, the JNA had a constitutional duty to defend the territorial integrity of the borders of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, especially due to the newly arisen circumstances and to the fact that the JNA commanders agreed to pull out of a number of Yugoslav territories, Slovenia, Croatia, and later also Bosnia-Herzegovina at a later stage. But there were a number of grave violations and a number of young recruits who were doing their regular military service got killed in the process.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did the SDA party view the JNA as being sympathetic to their cause?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I can't say. Perhaps you should ask one of the SDA people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Just to remind ourselves of what was happening 10 years ago, 11 years ago, on -- by the 30th of April, Bosnia had already declared its independence and had been recognised by the European Union and the United States. When you say it was the role of the JNA to defend the territory of Yugoslavia, are you saying it was their duty to prevent the secession of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Now, this is a predominantly political issue, and it's a very important issue. Part of the former Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia was in favour of saying in one state, and some other republics advocated the possibility of secession.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Let me just stop you. Please try to limit your answer to the question. My question was: When you say it was the role of the JNA to defend the territory of Yugoslavia, are you saying it was their duty to prevent the secession of Bosnia? Did you view the JNA's role as stopping Bosnia from seceding under the borders that were declared -- with the borders that were declared?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: The military leaders of the JNA, the part of the JNA that was in Bosnia and Herzegovina - I think it was General Kukanjac - they accepted the withdrawal of the army, and they never disputed the right of Bosnia and Herzegovina to be recognised as a state, although the constituent role of the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina had not been sufficiently determined. However, as the army was pulling its troops out and on their way to the territory that was still JNA controlled, these army convoys were often intercepted. Even the dispatch by Delimustafic was saying the same thing; it was stating the fact that this was indeed being done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, you haven't answered my question, and I'm going to move on and try to ask another one. Given what you knew about the political situation at that time, did the Muslims want the JNA to remain in Bosnia, the Muslim nationalists?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: The Muslim nationalists, I'm sure they wanted the JNA to leave Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And this telegram that you're talking about was from Delimustafic -- Minister Delimustafic instructing the police and interior minister forces -- ministry forces to stop the JNA from withdrawing. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Precisely -- yes. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, that telegram was denied -- the authenticity of that telegram was denied the next day by the presidency of Bosnia. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I want to go back to the Crisis Staff. Can you tell us under what legal authority the Crisis Staff was established. I'm not asking you as a lawyer, but to the best of your knowledge as a resident of Prijedor and the member of the assembly, what legal authority was cited in the establishment of that body?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: At a regular session of the assembly, the article of the assembly statute was discussed. And what this article envisaged was that when and if the assembly is unable to meet and continue work, a presidency of the assembly can be set up to continue work under a different set of circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. So when was the Crisis Staff established? Would I be correct in understanding that after the takeover, there no longer could be expected to be the Muslim and -- let me try to say this again. I'm sorry. Would I be correct that after the takeover, no one expected deputies of the assembly of Muslim and Croat nationality to come to the assembly meetings, so the assembly was no longer allowed to meet or was no longer -- it was no longer possible for the assembly to meet?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I must say this again. I don't know whether they were invited. I don't know whether they refused to continue to take part in the work of the assembly, and I don't know that perhaps they were not invited.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let me try to get at this another way. Sir, on the 30th of April, you were living in Prijedor and you were in Prijedor town that day. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Who was in charge of Prijedor on that day after the takeover? Who took over power?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I don't think the question is specific enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. On the 30th of April, President Cehajic, the president of the municipal assembly, was prevented from entering his office. We've been talking about a takeover of power on that day. Who took power?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I only learnt that something was going on when I was on my way to work. I could see the Serbian flag outside the municipal assembly building. And later I heard in the media, the local radio station, that there had been a takeover, and that with the exception of appointed officials -- elected officials, everyone else was free to go to work as usual. I remember President Cehajic's statement on the radio that he would put up Gandhi-like resistance, meaning that he would not take part in this whole thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. You said you heard an announcement in the radio about the takeover. Who did the announcement indicate was now the authority? What body replaced the previous government of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: The assembly met after that, and the document that you have been shown indicates who the new deputies were and that again -- once again, there were 90 deputies in the assembly. The assembly continued to work because the statute envisages that there have to be 90 deputies, and there could have been no interim elections in the sense of interim elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you recall when that -- when the assembly first met after the takeover? Was it the next day, the next week? Do you remember how long it took before this new assembly met?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I believe about 15 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Who was in control of Prijedor during those 15 days? Was the Crisis Staff already established and operating?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: The assembly does not meet that often. Usually it's enough for a parliament to meet -- to be convened once a month. The executive board and the executive authorities were perfectly free to go about their daily work until the next meeting of the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was it announced on the radio on the 30th of April that Dr. Stakic was the new president of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I don't think this was announced. I think 15 or 17 days later, like I said, it was announced at a session of the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, Dr. Stakic had already been elected by the SDS as the president of the Serbian Municipality of Prijedor prior to the takeover. They had separated and created their own shadow government, if you accept that term. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I don't know whether the SDS had a shadow government before that meeting of the assembly and whether Stakic was appointed the president of the municipal assembly, but I am sure that 15 or 17 days after the takeover such a decision was verified by the majority of the deputies at that particular session of the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And this was an assembly that included 60 members -- or excuse me, 62 members -- let me take it back. This included the SDS members of the -- that were elected in the 1990 elections, 13 members of the left bloc, I believe you said, and the rest, which I believe leaves 49, 49 newly-appointed deputies.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Appointed by the SDS, correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I don't know if all of them were appointed, because there was this group of ten others, and I believe that not all of them were SDS members.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember the posters that were around town that day after the takeover explaining the reasons for the takeover?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: On that day I was in my company in Ljubija and during that day I was not in the town anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In subsequent days, did you see posters in the town of Prijedor talking about the takeover and explaining the reasons for it?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I believe that there were posters, but I don't remember what they said. I don't remember the contents of those posters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you live in Ljubija or did you live in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I lived in Prijedor and I would commute to work in Ljubija. I would leave Prijedor in the morning, and I would come back in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Isn't it correct that those posters indicated that power had been taken by the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I really don't remember the contents of those posters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, you told us that Simo Drljaca was appointed by the interior minister --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Koumjian, that I interrupt, but I want to have a clarification. May I ask the witness once more: The 30th of April, you were in Prijedor town on that day. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's where I lived, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: On page 67 of today's transcript, you answered -- line 3: "Okay. Let me try to get at this another way. Sir, the question was: Sir, on the 30th of April, you were living in Prijedor and you were in Prijedor town that day. Is that correct?" Your answer was, "Yes."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 30th of April, I lived in Prijedor. At 7.00 in the morning I went to Ljubija to work, and I returned around 3.00 in the afternoon from Ljubija. So I was in Prijedor on that particular day up to 7.00 in the morning and after 3.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, what was the name of the interior minister that you indicated appointed Simo Drljaca as the chief of police in 1992?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I don't know the name of the minister, but I know for a fact that the minister was in charge of that appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Where was that minister physically located? Was he in Banja Luka? Was he in Pale? Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I don't know where his -- he was physically located.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Have you seen the order whereby the Minister of the Interior appointed Simo Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it a fact that the SDS elected Simo Drljaca to be the chief of police and this was published in Kozarski Vjesnik before the takeover -- the Prijedor SDS?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: What is certain is that the parties propose to the minister who should be appointed and it is the minister who nominates and appoints. It is not the local assembly that does it. It is the party that sends proposals to the minister, and the minister is the one who then appoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. So the nomination comes from the parties, correct, which is sent to the minister?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You cited one example in your direct examination of when a minister rejected the candidate proposed by the party, and that was Simo Miskovic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you cite any other example in Bosnia that you know of where the candidate of the party was rejected by the interior minister?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: As a deputy in the local assembly, I was not in the position to have the insight into the way candidates were nominated and appointed by the various ministers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. The example that you cited, Simo Miskovic, Mr. Miskovic did not have a university degree, and that was a requirement for the position to which he was the proposed chief of the traffic police. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: As far as I know, Miskovic used to work in the police and he also continued his education while he worked there. Whether at that particular time he had already graduated from the university or not, I don't know, and I don't know whether the reason for the rejection was the fact that he did not have the necessary qualification or something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So you don't know -- the answer would be you don't know whether or not he met the minimal qualifications for the position?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Yes, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do have a document -- I do have one document I would like to have distributed. It has not yet been marked, and it does not have a 65 ter number, but it does have this witness's name on it. It was previously disclosed to the Defence, and it has the ERN number of P0021922.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This would be provisionally as S394.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just for all parties' benefit, it's the third signature which I'm really interested in. I think the Court and counsel will recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, before my learned friend continues: I'm not sure if I heard him correctly or if the transcript was properly cited. Is the OTP saying they did give this document to us even though it didn't have a 65 ter number? And if so, just if you can share with us when it was that it was given to us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We're checking on the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: 28 May 2002. I think Mr. Ostojic was in Chicago that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask, do we have a translation or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We're checking on that. I do not believe this has ever been translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So therefore, it --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We'll request one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: An additional "B" should be added. It will be S394B [Realtime transcript read in error "P294B"].

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Could it be put on the ELMO, please, and shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, I believe you now have in front of you the document which we've marked -- I believe it should be S394B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise, first of all -- under the eighth signature, do you recognise your signature on this document?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And can you tell us what this document is briefly.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: In the preamble of this document, it says that the presidents of political parties and presidents of the groups of deputies at their meeting held on this date, in order to carry out the conclusions of the municipal assembly, at the 22nd January 1992 and with regard to the distribution of power, they have passed the following conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: There is a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Hmm?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: There is a translation, so we will have English by tomorrow morning, at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We'll try to get it now, but I think we are running out of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise the other signatures that appear on this document?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I recognise my signature and as for the others, I don't recognise them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Have you ever seen Dr. Stakic's signature before?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: No. The documents were stamped, and in the Official Gazettes there was no signature either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And in the Official Gazette, if next to the name the letters "SR" appear, can you explain what that means.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: It means that this is as if it was indeed signed by the person himself or herself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. The third signature, I'd ask you to just take a second and look at that. First of all, do you know Dragan Savanovic?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Dragan Savanovic was the president of the group of SDS deputies. And once the assembly was inaugurated, then he was the vice-president of the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Just so we're clear on the time period, after the takeover, following the 30th of April, Dragan Savanovic took the position of vice-president of the Serbian Municipal Assembly of Prijedor. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Now, if the president of the assembly is absent when a document needs to be signed, does the vice-president have the authority to sign on his behalf?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Yes. According to the statute, in the absence of the president, it is the vice-president who can sign a document, and this is in keeping with the laws and with the authorities of the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I want to switch to another topic now. You indicated that in 1993, Dr. Stakic resigned following pressure at the end of the previous year, 1992, from what you called the extreme wing of the SDS. Now, first, I understand that you never yourself participated in SDS meetings or discussions. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I didn't participate in any of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell me why you call this group "the extreme wing"? What was the difference in the policies advocated by those who forced Dr. Stakic or requested him to resign from Dr. Stakic's policies?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: During the session of the assembly before the SDA and HDZ deputies left the assembly, that wing of the SDS during the debates at the local parliament voiced harsher opinions that would make the relationships more acute in the parliament and elsewhere. This continued in the work of the new assembly. I don't know what were the reasons for that, but in any case the president, Stakic, was strongly attacked. They asked for more radical actions and more efficient work in that part of the work of the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What do you mean by "more radical actions"? Can you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I believe that they were not happy with the efficiency of work, and I believe that there were some party pressures. I don't know what the conclusions and pressures were all about, but at the sessions of the assembly one could notice that things had been discussed elsewhere and that the showdown time was at the sessions of the assembly and that the aim was to force Dr. Stakic to resign.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Were there allegations at that time that humanitarian aid had been misused, that it wasn't used for the correct purpose?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: The work of the humanitarian organisations, such as the Red Cross, Merhamet, Kolo Srpskih Sestara, and Dobrotvor, were under the authority of the representatives of the respective humanitarian organisations, and they did not report at -- to the local parliament on their work, neither did -- nor did the local parliament discuss their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, at the municipal assembly sessions, did you attend all the meetings that you were summoned to?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I believe that I did not attend all of them, but most of them I did attend. I can't give you the precise information as to which of them I didn't attend, but in any case I was present at over 80 per cent of the assembly sessions that were held.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: During those assembly sessions, did you discuss the detention of citizens of Prijedor in the Omarska and Keraterm camps? Let me just use a different word, because I don't want -- whatever word you want to call them, "camps," "collection centres," I just want to make sure we're talking about the same places. Did you discuss the detention of citizens of Prijedor at these places?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: This was not on the agenda of the assembly session, save for the report of the Crisis Staff that was presented to the assembly some two months into its work. Then they reported on the decisions made by the Crisis Staff. This was not an issue that was discussed, nor was it something that would be under the authority of the local assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, what did Dr. Stakic tell you about the Omarska and Keraterm camps?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: I was never in Dr. Stakic's company and at the sessions of the assembly this issue was not discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So just so I'm clear -- I believe I understand your answer. My question was not so specific. At the assembly sessions, you never heard Dr. Stakic discuss the Omarska or Keraterm camps. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Dr. Stakic never talked about that at any of the sessions of the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you told us, if I recall correctly, during your direct examination that you were present when the decisions of the Crisis Staff were later ratified by the municipal assembly in order to make them legal. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, have you ever heard the expression "the number one man in Prijedor"?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Would it be correct to describe the president of the municipal assembly as the number one man in Prijedor in political terms?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So if the journalist described him as "the number one man," that journalist would be misinformed?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: If a journalist had said that, I believe that he must have known why he said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Would the person in charge of the municipal -- I'm sorry, I don't recall the name of the secretariat -- the municipal services, the secretary for the municipal services. Would that individual --

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: The Secretariat for the General Administrative Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That person, would he be in a position to have a good idea of the powers and prestige of the office of president of the municipality -- of the municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: That person would sooner be able to say something about the work of the president of the executive board and the vice-president of the executive board because their work -- their respective jobs are interrelated. And as for the president of the municipal assembly, their contacts are very few, and whatever the secretary of that particular secretariat has to offer to the municipal, he does it through the executive board. So I don't see how they would get closely connected, the two of them through their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, what is the top position in the municipality -- let's be more specific. In 1992, what was the top political position in the Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: The building of the former League of Communists; in other words, the building of the social and political organisations lent its offices to a number of parties. Some of the parties had their headquarters elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't believe I stated my question clear enough. Which position was the most powerful political position in Prijedor in 1992?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: The most powerful executive position was of the president of the executive board. Now, as to the political power of a specific party or its leader, is reflected in the representation of that party in the government or in the authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, just one final question before the end of the night: In the agreement between the parties, the party that got the most votes, the most seats in the assembly, which position was allocated to them? Was it president of the executive board or was it the president of the municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VILA
utterances.text: The SDA was given the position of the president of the municipal assembly according to their interparty agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I could finish for the night, Your Honour. I have more questions for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it will take a lot of time. Let me just finish -- we should mark the English translation we just received as document S394A. But before I'm prepared to decide on the admission into evidence, on the one hand side I want to ask the Defence whether they can confirm that they received this document at the concrete point in time. On the other hand, I want to ask the Prosecution, please, as usual on these occasions, to provide us with the best possible original of S394B by tomorrow morning. This concludes your -- today's testimony. We will continue tomorrow at 9.00, but I have to ask you please do not contact any of the parties, be it the Prosecution or be it any member of this Defence team or another Defence team or any other person you identify as a may-be witness until we proceed here tomorrow at 9.00. Did you understand this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. The trial stays adjourned until tomorrow, 9.00, in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
